verdict.summary: You can connect your own account and up to 100 test users within minutes while the app is in Testing mode. Opening the app to anyone means Google verification. With Composio's default full-mailbox scope (https://mail.google.com/), that is restricted-scope review (about 6 weeks or more) plus a yearly third-party security assessment if Gmail data is stored on or sent through your servers. Sticking to narrow sensitive scopes such as gmail.send keeps you in a shorter review.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 30-60 min for Testing mode; 1-3 days of prep for verification (domain, privacy policy, video, justifications), plus security-assessment work if you use restricted scopes
verdict.approval_wait: None for Testing mode. Production: brand check 2-3 business days, sensitive scopes 3-10 business days, restricted scopes about 6 weeks (Google warns it can take several months). None of these estimates is guaranteed.

steps.title: Create a Google Cloud project
steps.detail: Sign in to Google Cloud Console with the account that will own the app, create a new project and enable the Gmail API for it. Use an account that will also be an owner or editor when you verify your domain later.
gotchas: The 100-user cap counts across the project's whole lifetime and cannot be reset. Use a fresh project for production rather than a heavily used test project.

steps.title: Decide on the narrowest Gmail scopes
steps.detail: List the Gmail actions your agent really needs and map each to the narrowest scope. For example, use gmail.send (sensitive) for send-only, not https://mail.google.com/ (restricted). Composio's default scope list includes https://mail.google.com/, which puts you on the restricted-scope verification path. Only keep it if you need IMAP/SMTP or full mailbox access.
gotchas: Google's policy says a send-only app shouldn't request full mailbox access, and reviewers ask why narrower scopes aren't enough.

steps.title: Configure the OAuth consent screen
steps.detail: In Google Auth Platform / OAuth consent screen, enter the app name, support email and developer contact. Choose External audience (or Internal if only your Workspace org will use it), and leave the publishing status as Testing. Use Add or remove scopes to declare every scope you picked; the picker sorts them into non-sensitive, sensitive and restricted groups.
gotchas: Internal apps skip the unverified-app screen and the 100-user cap, but only members of your Workspace org can use them.

steps.title: Create a Web application OAuth client with Composio's redirect URI
steps.detail: Under Credentials, choose Create credentials > OAuth client ID > Web application. Paste the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config under Authorized redirect URIs, then copy the Client ID and Client secret.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: The redirect URI must match exactly (scheme, host, path, trailing slash), or Google returns redirect_uri_mismatch.
Adding redirect URIs after verification triggers re-verification, so get them final first.

steps.title: Add test users
steps.detail: On the consent screen's Audience / Test users section, add your own Google account and any testers' accounts. Testing status allows up to 100 test users.
gotchas: Refresh tokens issued in Testing mode have a limited lifetime (reported as 7 days), so expect test connections to need re-authorization.

steps.title: Plug the client into Composio and run a test authorization
steps.detail: Create a Composio auth config for the gmail toolkit with your Client ID, Client secret and the scopes you chose, then start a connection and complete Google's consent with a test-user account. An invalid_client error means the client ID is wrong; redirect_uri_mismatch means the callback URL doesn't match.
gotchas: Test users will see the unverified-app screen before consent; this is expected until the app is verified.

steps.title: Publish a homepage and privacy policy on your own domain
steps.detail: Draft and publish a public homepage (not behind a login) and a privacy policy that says how the app accesses, uses, stores and shares Google user data, plus Terms of Service if you have them. Add these URLs to the consent screen branding.
gotchas: The policy must not allow Google user data to be used to train foundation or frontier AI models.

steps.title: Verify domain ownership in Search Console
steps.detail: Verify ownership of your homepage and privacy-policy domain in Google Search Console, using an account that is an owner or editor on the Cloud project. Google can't approve verification until this is done.

steps.title: Submit and publish brand verification
steps.detail: Submit brand verification from the Verification Center. Your branding status must be published before you can request data-access verification. Google estimates 2-3 business days.

steps.title: Prepare the demo video and scope justifications
steps.detail: Record a video showing a user starting the OAuth flow, granting consent and the app using each sensitive or restricted scope, and upload it to YouTube as unlisted. An agent can draft the written justification for each scope, explaining why narrower scopes aren't enough.

steps.title: Submit data access verification
steps.detail: Switch the publishing status to In production and submit data access verification in the Verification Center with the video link and justifications. Sensitive scopes need Google's review before any account can grant access without the unverified-app limits.

steps.title: Wait for Google's review
steps.detail: Google estimates 3-10 business days for sensitive scopes (its pages disagree) and about 6 weeks for restricted scopes, and warns sensitive-data verification can take several months. Answer reviewer emails quickly.

steps.title: Complete the security assessment (restricted scopes only)
steps.detail: If you use restricted scopes and store or send that data from servers, complete a security assessment with a Google-approved third-party assessor, and repeat it every year. Google charges no fee, but you agree a fee with the assessor (a third party reports about $540-$1k/yr for CASA Tier 2 self-serve).

steps.title: Keep the client active and compliant
steps.detail: Monitor usage on the OAuth user cap page, keep the client in use (Google may delete clients inactive for 6+ months), and avoid changing scopes, redirect URIs or the product name unless you're ready to re-verify. If you call Gmail through Google's MCP server, mark the OAuth client as an AI-agent client before November 11, 2026. Plain REST API use is not affected.

blockers.symptom: Users see 'Google hasn't verified this app' and new users are blocked once 100 have connected
blockers.cause: Unverified apps with sensitive or restricted scopes are capped at 100 new users over the project's lifetime.
blockers.fix: Complete verification, or use the Internal user type if every user is in your Workspace org. The cap can't be reset, so don't burn it on a test project you plan to ship.

blockers.cause: The redirect URI in the request doesn't exactly match one registered on the OAuth client.
blockers.fix: Paste Composio's callback URL exactly into Authorized redirect URIs.

blockers.cause: Restricted scopes stored on or sent through servers require an annual security assessment by a Google-approved assessor.
blockers.fix: Switch to narrower sensitive scopes (e.g., gmail.send) if you can, or budget for the assessor's fee and time.

blockers.symptom: Test connections stop working after a few days
blockers.cause: Refresh tokens in Testing mode have a limited lifetime (reported as 7 days).
blockers.fix: Re-authorize, or move to production with verification.

blockers.symptom: Verification rejected or revoked over AI use of data
blockers.cause: Google user data from sensitive or restricted scopes may not be used to train or improve foundation or frontier models.
blockers.fix: State in your privacy policy that you don't use the data this way, and make sure you actually don't.

blockers.symptom: Gmail MCP server rejects requests after Nov 11, 2026
blockers.cause: MCP servers reject OAuth clients that aren't marked as agentic.
blockers.fix: Mark the OAuth client as an AI-agent client if you use the Gmail MCP server. REST-only use is not affected.

blockers.cause: Google may delete clients inactive for 6+ months.
blockers.fix: Restore it within 30 days, and keep the client in use.

composio.note: Composio's managed Gmail OAuth app is the fastest way to prototype and avoids Google verification on your side. Register your own Google Cloud OAuth client when you need your own branding on the consent screen, your own quotas, or control over production. Don't copy Composio's default scopes into your own app: they include the restricted https://mail.google.com/ scope, which forces restricted-scope verification and possibly an annual security assessment. Request the narrowest Gmail scopes you need instead. Put Composio's callback URL into your client's Authorized redirect URIs.

open_questions: The findings don't describe the exact console flow for enabling the Gmail API in the project. Confirm it in the API Library.

Google's policy says redirect URIs should refer to domains you own. It's unclear how reviewers treat a Composio-hosted callback URL during verification, or whether Composio supports a white-labelled callback on your own domain.

The tiers of the People/Contacts scopes in Composio's default list (contacts.readonly, user.birthday.read, etc.) and of gmail.readonly/gmail.modify aren't confirmed on a Google page. Check them in the consent screen scope picker.
Google's own pages disagree on sensitive-scope review time (3-5 vs 10 business days vs several months).
The exact Testing-mode refresh-token lifetime (reported as 7 days) and any per-client refresh-token limit aren't confirmed by Google.
How to mark an OAuth client as agentic for the Gmail MCP server isn't detailed in the findings.
